# Discretely self-similar exterior-naked singularities for the Einstein-scalar field system

**Authors:** Serban Cicortas ††thanks: cicortas@princeton.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Fine Hall, Washington Road, Princeton NJ 08544, United States of America Christoph Kehle ††thanks: kehle@mit.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Building 2, 77 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA 02139, United States of America

## Abstract

The problem of constructing naked singularities in general relativity can be naturally divided into two parts:

the construction of the region exterior to the past light cone of the singularity, extending all the way to (an incomplete) future null infinity and yielding the nakedness property (what we will call exterior-naked singularity regions)

attaching an interior fill-in that ensures that the singularity arises from regular initial data.

This problem has been resolved for the spherically symmetric Einstein-scalar field system by Christodoulou [Chr94], but his construction, based on a continuously self-similar ansatz, requires that both the exterior and the interior regions are mildly irregular on the past cone of the singularity. On the other hand, numerical works suggest that there exist naked singularity spacetimes with discrete self-similarity arising from smooth initial data. In this paper, we revisit part (i) of the problem and we construct exterior-naked singularity regions with discretely self-similar profiles which are smooth on the past cone of the singularity. We show that the scalar field remains uniformly bounded, but the singularity is characterized by the infinite oscillations of the scalar field and the mass aspect ratio. (Our examples require however that the mass aspect ratio is uniformly small, and thus the solutions are distinct from the exterior regions of the numerical examples.) It remains an open problem to smoothly attach interior fill-ins as in (ii) to our solutions, which would yield a new construction of naked singularity spacetimes, now arising from smooth initial data.

## 1 Introduction

The Einstein-scalar field system

$$ \begin{cases}Ric_{\mu\nu}=2\partial_{\mu}\phi\partial_{\nu}\phi\\
\square_{g}\phi=0\end{cases} $$

for a spherically symmetric spacetime $\big(M^{3+1},g\big)$ and a scalar field $\phi$ is a well-established model for studying the physics of gravitational collapse [Chr71]. The spacetime $\big(M^{3+1},g\big)$ admits double null coordinates $(u,v,\vartheta,\varphi)$ such that the metric takes the form

$$ g=-\Omega^{2}(u,v)dudv+r^{2}(u,v)d\sigma_{S^{2}}, $$

where $d\sigma_{S^{2}}\doteq d\vartheta^{2}+\sin^{2}\vartheta d\varphi^{2}$ is the standard metric on the sphere $S^{2}$ and the function $r(u,v)$ is the area radius of the orbits of the $SO(3)$ action.

For asymptotically flat spherically symmetric initial data for (1.1), solutions arising from small data disperse to Minkowski space, while there exist large-data solutions that contain a black hole region. A third class of solutions that play a special role are naked singularity spacetimes. Informally, these spacetimes contain a singularity that is visible to far away observers and not hidden behind the event horizon of a black hole. An alternative way to think about naked singularities is that they cause the incompleteness of future null infinity $\mathcal{I}^{+},$ which represents the set of idealized far away observers. It is well-known that such a singularity, denoted by $b_{\Gamma}$ , can only form at the center $\{r=0\}$ and the past lightcone $C_{0}^{-}$ of $b_{\Gamma}$ naturally divides a naked singularity spacetime into an exterior-naked singularity region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ and an interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ , see Fig. 1. It is precisely the geometry of the exterior region that determines the nakedness of the singularity, while the interior fill-in ensures that the spacetime arises dynamically from regular collapse.

The incompleteness of $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ of naked singularity spacetimes constitutes a failure of global existence for far away observers and threatens the predictability of general relativity. The weak cosmic censorship conjecture, originally formulated by Penrose in [Pen69] for more general Einstein-matter systems, postulates that, generically, naked singularities do not form and $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ is complete [GH78, Chr99]. In the seminal work [Chr99a], Christodoulou proved the conjecture for (1.1) in spherical symmetry. We shall return to this work in Section 1.5.

*Figure 1: Penrose diagram of a spacetime with future incomplete $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ and a naked singularity at $b_{\Gamma}$ arising from data on $C_{0}^{+}$ . The past ingoing light cone of the singularity $b_{\Gamma}$ is denoted with $C_{0}^{-}$ and divides the spacetime into the exterior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ and the interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ .*

The genericity condition in formulating the weak cosmic censorship conjecture is indeed necessary because naked singularity spacetimes have been shown to form dynamically for (1.1) in spherical symmetry. We describe two kinds of naked singularities below, which can be classified as featuring continuous self-similarity and discrete self-similarity. The continuously self-similar solutions were rigorously constructed, while the discretely self-similar solutions have been obtained only numerically. We refer to Fig. 2 for an illustration highlighting the differences between continuous and discrete self-similarity.

#### Continuous self-similarity.

In [Chr94], Christodoulou constructed naked singularities based on a continuous self-similar ansatz for the solution. The singular nature of the spacetimes is a result of the blow-up of the scalar field towards $b_{\Gamma}$ along the ingoing self-similar cone $C_{0}^{-}$ . The additional continuous symmetry reduces the PDE system (1.1) to an autonomous ODE system, which plays an essential role in the construction. The proof is divided into two parts:

- (i) the construction of the exterior-naked singularity region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$

- (ii) attaching an interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ .

In each region, the solution is obtained from a suitable orbit of the autonomous ODE system. A key feature of Christodoulou’s examples is the limited regularity on the past cone of the singularity. In particular, the exterior-naked singularity region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ is already mildly irregular at $C_{0}^{-}$ . Thus, when viewed in the context of the Cauchy problem, the data have an initial mild singularity at $C_{0}^{-}\cap C_{0}^{+}$ . We refer to Section 1.4 for a more detailed discussion. These naked singularities have been generalized recently in [Sin24] to solutions with an asymptotically continuous self-similar profile. The strategy of dividing the problem into (i) and (ii) is also used in the recent groundbreaking work [RS23, Shl22] of Rodnianski and Shlapentokh-Rothman who constructed naked singularities for the Einstein vacuum equations, necessarily outside of spherical symmetry, for which the continuous self-similarity is generalized to a twisted self-similarity. We will discuss this work in more detail in Section 1.4.

#### Discrete self-similarity.

In the numerical study [Cho93] on critical gravitational collapse for (1.1), Choptuik first observed naked singularities with asymptotically discretely self-similar symmetry to occur on the black hole formation threshold—the interface in the moduli space of solutions between dispersion and collapse. In these spacetimes, the singularity is caused by bounded infinite oscillations of the scalar field along the past light cone $C_{0}^{-}$ of the singular point $b_{\Gamma}$ . Further numerical studies showed that all naked singularity solutions obtained using Choptuik’s procedure asymptote to a universal solution with exact discretely self-similar symmetry as the singularity $b_{\Gamma}$ is approached, see the review article [GM07]. We refer to this conjectured universal solution as the conjectured Choptuik solution. Note that in view of the exact discrete self-similarity, the conjectured Choptuik solution would not itself be asymptotically flat, although it would occur as the limit of asymptotically flat solutions as the singularity is approached.

### 1.1 The main theorem: construction of exterior-naked singularity regions

To date, no rigorous construction of discretely self-similar naked singularities has been achieved. As explained above, all examples to date have continuous self-similar symmetry and are of limited regularity. The difficulty arises from the fact that, unlike continuous self-similarity, imposing discrete self-similarity does not reduce the system to ODEs and one is still faced with a system of PDEs.

The main result of this paper is to address part (i) of the strategy outlined above and construct a class of exterior-naked singularity regions $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ with discretely self-similar profile along $C_{0}^{-}$ arising from initial data which are moreover smooth away from the singularity.

#### Theorem 1.

For any $\Delta>0$ , there exist spherically symmetric exterior-naked singularity solutions to (1.1) in the region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}\doteq\{-1\leq u<0,\ v\geq 0\}$ with a future incomplete $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ and a Penrose diagram as depicted in Fig. 3. In addition, the following hold.

- 1. The solutions are smooth in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ , in particular up to and including the ingoing cone $C^{-}_{0}:=[-1,0)\times\{0\}$ , i.e. they are smooth away from the singularity $b_{\Gamma}:=(0,0)$ .

- 2. Along the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ , the solutions satisfy the discrete self-similarity properties

$$ \phi\circ\theta_{\Delta}=\phi,\quad\mu\circ\theta_{\Delta}=\mu,\quad\frac{\partial_{v}\phi}{\partial_{v}r}\circ\theta_{\Delta}=e^{\Delta}\frac{\partial_{v}\phi}{\partial_{v}r}, $$

(1.3) where $\theta_{\Delta}(u,0)=(e^{-\Delta}u,0)$ and the gauge condition $r|_{C_{0}^{-}}=-u$ holds.

- 3. The scalar field $\phi$ and the mass aspect ratio $\mu=\frac{2m}{r}\doteq 1+4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}r$ remain small in amplitude

$$ \sup_{C_{0}^{-}}|\phi|\ll_{\Delta}1,\quad\sup_{C_{0}^{-}}|\mu|\ll_{\Delta}1 $$

(1.4) but undergo infinite oscillations along $C_{0}^{-}$ as the singularity $b_{\Gamma}$ is approached.

*Figure 3: Penrose diagram of an exterior-naked singularity region constructed in Theorem 1. Along the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ , the solution is discretely self-similar and satisfies (1.3). The singularity at $b_{\Gamma}$ is characterized by the infinite but uniformly bounded oscillations of the scalar field $\phi$ and the mass aspect ratio $\mu$ towards $b_{\Gamma}$ .*

#### Remark 1.1.

The solutions constructed in Theorem 1 have an exactly discretely self-similar profile only along the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ and are approximately discretely self-similar away from $C_{0}^{-}$ . We note that constructing spacetimes with asymptotically flat null infinity $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ requires the data on $C_{0}^{+}$ to be asymptotically flat, which is incompatible with global discrete self-similarity. However, one should be able to produce non-asymptotically flat spacetimes with exact discrete self-similarity using the extracting procedure of [RS18, Theorem 1.2]. These would still have the Penrose diagram of Fig. 3, but would not satisfy the usual notions of asymptotical flatness at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ , as for instance the Bondi mass would diverge there.

### 1.2 Attaching an interior fill-in and constructing a naked singularity from smooth data

Our main result provides a construction of an exterior-naked singularity region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}},$ while it remains an open problem to construct an appropriate interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ , in the past of $C_{0}^{-}$ .

#### Open problem.

Does any of the exterior-naked singularity regions constructed in Theorem 1 admit an interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ which can be attached smoothly to obtain a naked singularity spacetime $\mathcal{R}_{\rm Int}\cup\mathcal{R}_{\rm Ext}$ as depicted in Fig. 1?

We stress that our exterior-naked singularity regions are fundamentally different from those numerically observed by Choptuik in [Cho93]. Specifically, the naked singularities in Choptuik’s simulations are incompatible with the smallness condition (1.4).

A natural way to construct an interior solution $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ is to make an exactly discrete self-similar ansatz in the interior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ . Since the self-similar vector field (see already (1.14))

$$ S=u\partial_{u}+(1-\kappa)v\partial_{v} $$

is timelike in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ , this requires constructing periodic-in-time solutions to hyperbolic PDEs. On the other hand, in the region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ which is successfully constructed in Theorem 1, the vector field $S$ is spacelike, and we have to construct approximately periodic-in-space solutions. (For the construction in the exterior region there are robust techniques available, even outside spherical symmetry [RS23], to which we return in Section 1.4.)

An additional challenge in smoothly attaching an interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ to the exterior-naked singularity regions of Theorem 1 follows from the extension principle of Christodoulou [Chr93, Theorem 5.1], applied to solutions that are at least $C^{2}$ regular. By the extension principle, for any such interior fill-in, the mass aspect ratio $\mu$ cannot satisfy the smallness bounds (1.4) globally on $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ , and there would have to be a region in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ where $\mu\sim 1$ .

### 1.3 The black hole formation threshold and the conjectured Choptuik solution

We recall that the numerical simulations in [Cho93] suggest that the black hole formation threshold consists of asymptotically discretely self-similar naked singularities which asymptote to a universal solution—the conjectured Choptuik solution. Based on these numerics we formulate the following open problem.

#### Open problem.

Does the black hole formation threshold consist of asymptotically discretely self-similar naked singularities? If so, do all such naked singularities asymptote to a universal discretely self-similar solution—the conjectured Choptuik solution—as the singularity is approached?

A natural first problem in addressing the above is constructing a possible candidate for the conjectured Choptuik solution. Indeed, based on the numerical simulations in [Cho93], the work [RT19] gives a computer-assisted construction of a smooth, discretely self-similar, spherically symmetric solution to (1.1), defined however only in an open neighborhood of the causal past of an ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ with singular vertex. If it can be proved that one can smoothly attach an exterior discretely self-similar solution, the construction would correspond to a natural candidate for the conjectured Choptuik solution.11 1 By an easy truncation argument in the far region one could then produce asymptotically flat examples, and this would then show the formation of naked singularities from smooth asymptotically flat initial data.

### 1.4 Comparison with the $k$ -self-similar solutions and the vacuum case

We compare the solutions of Theorem 1 with the naked singularity spacetimes of Christodoulou [Chr94] and the examples of Rodnianski and Shlapentokh-Rothman [RS23, Shl22]. Since we construct only exterior-naked singularity regions in Theorem 1, we restrict our comparison to the exterior regions in [Chr94] and [RS23] and the behavior on the past light cone of the singularity.

As discussed before, the $k$ -self-similar spacetimes constructed in [Chr94] are continuously self-similar solutions of (1.1) and have naked singularities for a certain range of the parameter $k.$ Along the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ , the $k$ -self-similar solutions satisfy

$$ \phi=kt+O(1),\ \mu=\frac{k^{2}}{1+k^{2}}, $$

where $t\doteq-\log|u|$ denotes the self-similar time. Thus, the singularity is a consequence of the blow-up of the scalar field and the failure of the mass aspect ratio to converge to zero. This is in contrast to the solutions constructed in Theorem 1 for which the scalar field and mass aspect ratio are periodic (see (1.3)) along $C_{0}^{-}$ in terms of the self-similar variable $t$ and the singularity is a consequence of this infinite oscillation.

In the works [RS23, Shl22], the first examples of the dynamical formation of naked singularities for the Einstein vacuum equations were constructed. The solutions have a twisted self-similar symmetry along $C_{0}^{-}$ , which represents a novel continuously self-similar mechanism for singularity formation, see also [Shl23]. The construction of the exterior-naked singularity regions in [RS23] is similar to that in Theorem 1 in many aspects. In both spacetimes the singularity is caused by a self-similar profile on $C_{0}^{-},$ with the infinite twisting of the geometry in [RS23] being replaced by the infinite oscillation in Theorem 1. However, the exterior regions are not assumed to have an exact self-similar symmetry in the future of $C_{0}^{-}$ , and they turn out to be only asymptotically self-similar. For both constructions the strategy is to first prescribe characteristic initial data compatible with the self-similar symmetry on $C_{0}^{-}$ and then prove global existence of the solution. We note that the guideline of [RS23] is the natural approach to construct exterior-naked singularity regions, in the case where the system of equations does not reduce to ODEs as in [Chr94].

In terms of the regularity of the spacetimes, there is a stark contrast between the solutions of Theorem 1 and the examples of [Chr94] and [RS23, Shl22]. In agreement with the numerical heuristics for discretely self-similar spacetimes, the solutions of Theorem 1 are globally smooth, except for $\{u=0\}$ of course. In particular, the solutions are smooth at $C_{0}^{-}.$ On the other hand, for the $k$ -self-similar and twisted self-similar examples of naked singularities, the construction of the exterior region already restricts the regularity of the spacetime to $C_{v}^{1,\gamma}$ for some $\gamma>0$ at $C_{0}^{-}$ , while the solution is smooth away from $C_{0}^{-}$ .

The solutions of Theorem 1 arise from small data by construction. Even though the infinite oscillation of the mass aspect ratio $\mu$ on $C_{0}^{-}$ causes the singularity, we obtain that $\mu$ is everywhere small, which is essential in the proof of global existence. On the other hand, the solutions of [Chr94] do not have any restrictions on the smallness of data, and global existence is obtained by the study of an autonomous ODE system. Finally, the solutions of [RS23] are in a large data regime on $C_{0}^{-}$ . Global existence is achieved since the initial data on $C_{0}^{+}$ decays rapidly away from $C_{0}^{-}$ , but this is done at the cost of the aforementioned limited Hölder regularity along $C_{0}^{-}$ .

### 1.5 The instability of naked singularities

In [Chr99a], Christodoulou showed that all naked singularity solutions to (1.1) are unstable, thereby proving the weak cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein-scalar field system in spherical symmetry. The precise formulation of his result required a low regularity class of initial perturbations. The argument crucially relies on rough perturbations that trigger a blue-shift instability along the cone $C_{0}^{-},$ which inevitably leads to the formation of trapped surfaces. Moreover, we note that the continuously self-similar naked singularity solutions in [Chr94] belong to the low regularity class considered, so the genericity assumption in the formulation of weak cosmic censorship in the low regularity class is indeed necessary. In the smooth class, both the question of the formation of naked singularities and the question of their genericity remain open. In view of the recent linear analysis in [Sin24a], the latter appears to be a very subtle and intricate problem.

### 1.6 Outline of the proof of Theorem 1

In the following, we will outline the main ideas used in the proof of Theorem 1. We begin by writing down the system of equations (1.1) in spherical symmetry expressed in double null coordinates which reduces to the wave equations

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}\partial_{v}\log\Omega^{2} \displaystyle=-2\partial_{u}\phi\partial_{v}\phi+\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2r^{2}}+\frac{2\partial_{v}r\partial_{u}r}{r^{2}} \displaystyle\partial_{u}(r\partial_{v}r) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{4}\Omega^{2} \displaystyle r\partial_{u}\partial_{v}\phi \displaystyle=-\partial_{v}\phi\partial_{u}r-\partial_{u}\phi\partial_{v}r $$

and the Raychaudhuri equations

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{u}r) \displaystyle=-r\Omega^{-2}(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2} \displaystyle\partial_{v}(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r) \displaystyle=-r\Omega^{-2}(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}. $$

Moreover, the Hawking mass

$$ m\doteq\frac{r}{2}(1+4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r\partial_{u}r) $$

satisfies

$$ \partial_{v}m=2r^{2}\Omega^{-2}(-\partial_{u}r)(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}. $$

#### Discretely self-similar characteristic data (Section 2).

We will set up smooth characteristic initial data on the cones $C_{0}^{-}\cup_{p}C_{0}^{+}=\{-1\leq u<0\}\times\{v=0\}\cup\{u=-1\}\times\{v\geq 0\}$ , which intersect at the sphere located at $p=(-1,0)$ . Characteristic data for the system (1.1) consist of prescribing $r,\Omega,\phi$ which satisfy (1.8) on $C_{0}^{-}$ and (1.9) on $C_{0}^{+},$ together with suitable gauge conditions, see Section 2.1.

The starting point in our construction is to consider smooth, discretely self-similar functions $\phi:C_{0}^{-}\times\{0\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ satisfying

$$ \kappa\Delta=\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}(-u^{\prime})\big(\partial_{u}\phi\big)^{2}du^{\prime} $$

for some small constant $0<\kappa\ll 1$ as well as the additional pointwise bounds

$$ \phi(e^{-\Delta}u,0)=\phi(u,0),\ |\phi(u,0)|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa},\ |\partial_{u}\phi(u,0)|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}/|u|. $$

The parameter $\kappa$ in (1.11) can be seen as the analog of $k^{2}$ in the $k$ -self-similar spacetimes in [Chr94].

The lapse function $\Omega^{2}$ is determined by $\phi$ on $C_{0}^{-}$ according to (1.8), and satisfies the scaling relation

$$ \Omega^{2}(e^{-\Delta n}u,0)=e^{-n\Delta\kappa}\Omega^{2}(u,0). $$

We remark that the scaling of $\Omega^{2}$ implies that the underlying vector field which determines the self-similar scaling (1.3) is given by

$$ S=u\partial_{u}+(1-\kappa)v\partial_{v}. $$

Enforcing the discrete self-similarity (1.3) along $C_{0}^{-}$ introduces rigidity conditions on the outgoing data on $C_{0}^{+}$ to first order at $p$ . In particular, from the discrete self-similarity property (1.3), equations (1.6) and (1.7), we obtain that the transverse derivatives $\partial_{v}r$ and $\partial_{v}\phi$ at $p$ are completely determined by the data on $C_{0}^{-}$ .22 2 We are only concerned with discrete self-similarity to first order at $C_{0}^{-}$ , but higher order versions of (1.3) would lead to higher order rigidity for the transverse derivatives at $p$ . An essential aspect of our discretely self-similar construction is that the rigidity condition give us the smallness properties

$$ \big|\partial_{v}\phi(p)\big|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa},\quad\mu(p)\lesssim\kappa. $$

This is in contrast with the $k$ -self-similar spacetimes in [Chr94], where the outgoing data $\partial_{v}\phi(p)$ is of size $1/k,$ which is never small in the range of the parameter $k$ . At higher order on $C_{0}^{+}$ , we have the freedom to prescribe $\phi$ smoothly33 3 Our proof also works if $\phi$ is at least $C^{1,\gamma}_{v}\big([0,\infty)\big)$ regular, where $\gamma=2\kappa/(1-\kappa).$ This is the same regularity exponent as in [RS23]., provided that certain smallness properties and asymptotically flat conditions hold.

#### Construction of the exterior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ (Section 3).

Once we set up the characteristic initial data, we prove that it leads to a global solution in the exterior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ . Our argument for global existence follows the strategy of [RS23] and relies only on the smallness of the initial data and bounds compatible with self-similarity, without requiring the solution to be exactly self-similar. In our proof, we decompose the spacetime into certain regions, and use bootstrap arguments to show suitable pointwise estimates for the solution in each region. In the last step, these bounds are then used to prove that $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ is incomplete, so the spacetime constructed represents indeed an exterior-naked singularity region.

We consider a small constant $\underline{v}$ such that $0<\kappa\ll\underline{v}\ll 1$ , and the regions depicted in Fig. 4

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{I} \displaystyle=\bigg\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[0,\underline{v}^{1-\kappa}],\ \frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\leq\underline{v}^{1-\kappa}\bigg\} \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{II} \displaystyle=\bigg\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[0,\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}],\ \underline{v}^{1-\kappa}\leq\frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\leq\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}\bigg\} \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{III} \displaystyle=\bigg\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[0,1],\ \frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\geq\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}\bigg\} \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{IV} \displaystyle=\bigg\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[1,\infty),\ \frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\geq\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}\bigg\}. $$

*Figure 4: The decomposition of $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ into the regions $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ – $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$*

In region $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ , we propagate the pointwise bounds on the solution on the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-},$ using the smallness of $\underline{v}.$ The estimates are straightforward for the quantities satisfying transport equations in the $\partial_{v}$ direction, such as $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r,\ \partial_{u}\phi,\ \partial_{u}r,$ and $\partial_{u}\log\Omega^{2}.$ On the other hand, in order to bound $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi$ we integrate the $\partial_{u}$ equation satisfied by $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi(u,v)-\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi(u,0).$

In regions $\mathcal{R}_{II}$ , $\mathcal{R}_{III}$ , and $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ , we consider the regular change of coordinates $V=v^{\frac{1}{1-\kappa}}$ motivated by the scaling vector field $S$ in (1.14), and we denote the new lapse function by $\bar{\Omega}.$ We prove estimates in region $\mathcal{R}_{II}$ by conjugating the equations with $\exp\big(D\cdot V/u\big)$ , for some large constant $D.$ These estimates are analogous to applying a local-in-time energy estimate in the “time” variable $V/u$ , with data on the spacelike hypersurface $\big\{V=-\underline{v}u\big\}.$

In region $\mathcal{R}_{III}$ we prove pointwise estimates using the smallness of $\underline{v}$ for the quantities satisfying transport equations in the $\partial_{u}$ direction, such as $\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\partial_{u}r,\ \partial_{V}\phi,\ \partial_{V}r,$ and $\partial_{V}\log\bar{\Omega}^{2}.$ However, in order to bound $\partial_{u}\phi,$ we conjugate the equation for $r\partial_{u}\phi$ by $|u|^{p}/V^{p},$ for some small constant $p>0.$ In particular, we obtain that $\phi\in C_{u}^{1-p}$ , but we cannot conclude that $\partial_{u}\phi$ and $\bar{\Omega}$ extend continuously to $\{u=0\}.$ Nevertheless, the quantitative bounds obtained will suffice for our purposes.

We prove estimates in region $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ using the a priori bound on the Hawking mass obtained from the initial data bound and the monotonicity properties. It is convenient to split region $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ into two sub-regions: $\mathcal{R}_{IV}\cap\{v\leq\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}\}$ with similar pointwise bounds to those of region $\mathcal{R}_{III}$ , and $[-1,0)\times[\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa},\infty)$ with bounds specific to an asymptotically flat region. Finally, we then use the estimates in region $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ to show that $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ is incomplete.

## 2 Discretely self-similar characteristic data

The characteristic initial data are given by $r,\Omega,\phi$ which satisfy Raychaudhuri’s equations (1.8) on $C_{0}^{-}$ and (1.9) on $C_{0}^{+}.$ In this section we set up suitable characteristic initial data, which are consistent with ingoing discrete self-similarity along $C_{0}^{-}$ and asymptotic flatness along $C_{0}^{+}.$

### 2.1 Underlying manifold and gauge conditions

We will consider the maximal globally hyperbolic development of data imposed on the bifurcate double null cones $C_{0}^{-}=\{-1\leq u<0\}\times\{v=0\}$ and $C_{0}^{+}=\{u=-1\}\times\{0\leq v<\infty\}$ . The bifurcation sphere is $p=\{u=-1\}\times\{v=0\}.$ We will denote the future domain of dependence of $C_{0}^{-}\cup_{p}C_{0}^{+}$ with $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ext}}=\{-1\leq u<0\}\times\{0\leq v<\infty\}$ .

On the incoming cone $C_{0}^{-}$ we impose

$$ r(u,0)=-u. $$

This can be interpreted as choosing the gauge condition $\partial_{u}r=-1$ along $C_{0}^{-}$ and $r(p)=1$ . We also impose that $\phi(p)=0$ .

On the outgoing cone $C_{0}^{+}$ we impose the gauge

$$ \partial_{v}\Omega^{2}=0. $$

This fixes the gauge upon specifying $\Omega^{2}(p)$ which will be done later. We are now in the position of defining characteristic data with ingoing discrete self-similarity.

### 2.2 Characteristic data with ingoing discrete self-similarity

#### Definition 2.1 (Characteristic data with ingoing discrete self-similarity).

Let $N>0$ be a regularity index for the tangential derivatives. We say that the seed $\phi(\cdot,0):C_{0}^{-}\to\mathbb{R}$ , $\phi(0,\cdot)\colon C_{0}^{+}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\phi(p)=0$ gives rise to a $C^{N}$ -regular characteristic data set on $C_{0}^{-}\cup_{p}C_{0}^{+}$ with ingoing discrete self-similarity if there exist constants $\Delta>0$ , $0<\kappa<1$ , and $C_{data}>0$ such that upon specifying

$$ \Omega^{2}(p)=\frac{1}{1-\kappa} $$

and imposing the gauge conditions from Section 2.1, the following conditions hold:

- 1. The scalar field satisfies $\phi(\cdot,0)\in C^{N+1}(C_{0}^{-})$ and $\phi(0,\cdot)\in C^{N+1}(C_{0}^{+})$ .

- 2. The scalar field is discretely self-similar on $C_{0}^{-}$ , i.e.,

$$ \phi(e^{-\Delta}u,0)=\phi(u,0). $$

(2.3)

- 3. The constant $\kappa$ satisfies

$$ \kappa=\frac{F(-e^{-\Delta})}{\Delta}, $$

(2.4) where

$$ F(u)\doteq\int_{-1}^{u}(-u^{\prime})\big(\partial_{u}\phi(u^{\prime},0)\big)^{2}du^{\prime}. $$

(2.5)

- 4. The scalar field satisfies the self-similar bounds

$$ \ |\phi(u,0)|\leq C_{data}\sqrt{\kappa},\ |\partial_{u}\phi(u,0)|\leq C_{data}\sqrt{\kappa}|u|^{-1} $$

(2.6) on $C_{0}^{-}$ .

- 5. The mass aspect ratio $\mu\doteq\frac{2m}{r}$ is discretely self-similar on $C_{0}^{-}$ , i.e.,

$$ \mu(e^{-\Delta}u,0)=\mu(u,0). $$

(2.7)

- 6. The first transverse derivatives of the scalar field and of the radiation field are discretely self-similar along $C_{0}^{-}$

$$ \frac{\partial_{v}(r\phi)}{\partial_{v}r}(e^{-\Delta}u,0)=\frac{\partial_{v}(r\phi)}{\partial_{v}r}(u,0) $$

(2.8) and

$$ \frac{\partial_{v}\phi}{\partial_{v}r}(e^{-\Delta}u,0)=e^{\Delta}\frac{\partial_{v}\phi}{\partial_{v}r}(u,0). $$

(2.9)

- 7. The scalar field satisfies the asymptotically flat conditions on $C_{0}^{+}$

$$ \big|\partial_{v}\phi(-1,v)\big|\leq C_{data}\sqrt{\kappa}\cdot\frac{1}{(1+v)^{2}},\quad\big|\partial_{v}^{2}\phi(-1,v)\big|\leq C_{data}\sqrt{\kappa}\cdot\frac{1}{(1+v)^{3}}. $$

(2.10)

#### Remark 2.2.

The equation (2.4) can also be regarded as a definition of $\kappa$ which measures the size of $\phi$ along $C_{0}^{-}$ . In our construction, we will take $\kappa$ to be a small quantity.

#### Remark 2.3.

Note that $\Omega^{2}$ and the transverse derivatives $\partial_{v}r$ and $\partial_{v}\phi$ along $C_{0}^{-}$ are determined by their values at the bifurcation sphere $p$ and (1.6)–(1.8). We will prove in Lemma 2.7 and Lemma 2.8 in Section 2.3 that for discretely self-similar data as in Definition 2.1, the values $\partial_{v}r(p)$ and $\partial_{v}\phi(p)$ are rigid.

The statement that there exist non-trivial characteristic data with ingoing discrete self-similarity as defined in Definition 2.1 is the content of the following proposition, which will be proved in Section 2.4.

#### Proposition 2.4.

For any $\Delta>0$ , there exists a $C_{data}=C_{data}(\Delta)>0$ such that for any $\kappa>0$ , and $N\geq 1$ , there exists a non-trivial seed function $\phi\colon C_{0}^{-}\cup_{p}C_{0}^{+}\to\mathbb{R}$ giving rise to $C^{k}$ -regular characteristic data with ingoing self-similarity as defined in Definition 2.1.

### 2.3 Consequences of imposing discrete self-similarity

In Section 2 we use the following convention. For non-negative quantities $A$ and $B$ , we write $A\lesssim B$ if there exists a constant $\tilde{C}>0$ only depending on $C_{data}$ and $\Delta$ from Definition 2.1 such that $A\leq\tilde{C}B$ . We will also write “for sufficiently small $0<\kappa\ll 1$ ” if there exists a constant $\kappa_{0}>0$ sufficiently small and only depending on $C_{data}$ , $\Delta$ from Definition 2.1 such that $\kappa$ satisfies $0<\kappa\leq\kappa_{0}$ .

#### 2.3.1 Estimates and rigidity along the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$

As a consequence of discrete self-similarity along $C_{0}^{-}$ , we prove rigidity for the lapse $\Omega^{2}$ in Lemma 2.5 and Lemma 2.6. We also prove rigidity for $\partial_{v}r$ and $\partial_{v}\phi$ on $C_{0}^{-}$ in Lemma 2.7 and Lemma 2.8, which in particular determines the outgoing data on $C_{0}^{+}$ to first order at $p.$

#### Lemma 2.5.

Consider discretely self-similar data as in Definition 2.1. Then, the function $F$ as defined in (2.5) satisfies

$$ F(-1)=0,\quad F(e^{-n\Delta}u)=F(u)+n\kappa\Delta. $$

for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and

$$ \sup_{u\in[-1,0)}\Big|\frac{F(u)}{\log|u|}\Big|\lesssim\kappa,\quad\left|\frac{d}{du}F(u)\right|\lesssim\kappa|u|^{-1},\ \left|\log\big(|u|^{-\kappa}e^{-F(u)}\big)\right|\lesssim\kappa. $$

#### Proof.

We compute

$$ \displaystyle F(u) \displaystyle=\int_{-1}^{u}(-u^{\prime})(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2}du^{\prime}=\int_{-e^{-\Delta}}^{e^{-\Delta}u}(-e^{\Delta}u^{\prime})(e^{-\Delta}\partial_{u}\phi)^{2}e^{\Delta}du^{\prime} \displaystyle=\int_{-1}^{e^{-\Delta}u}(-u^{\prime})(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2}du^{\prime}-\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}(-u^{\prime})(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2}du^{\prime}=F(e^{-\Delta}u)-\kappa\Delta, $$

where we used a change of variables, (2.3) and (2.4). Iterating this yields (2.11). The bounds (2.12) are a direct consequence of (2.6) and (2.11). ∎

#### Lemma 2.6.

Consider self-similar data as in Definition 2.1. Then, the lapse $\Omega^{2}(u,0)$ on $C_{0}^{-}$ is uniquely determined as

$$ \Omega^{2}(u,0)=\frac{1}{1-\kappa}e^{-F(u)}, $$

where $F$ is defined in (2.5). In particular,

$$ \Omega^{2}(e^{-\Delta n}u,0)=e^{-n\Delta\kappa}\Omega^{2}(u,0). $$

#### Proof.

By our gauge condition on $C_{0}^{-}$ we have $\partial_{u}r=-1$ . Thus, (1.8) reads

$$ \partial_{u}(\Omega^{-2})=-u\Omega^{-2}(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2} $$

or

$$ \partial_{u}\log\Omega^{2}=u(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2} $$

which shows (2.13) upon integration and using (2.5). ∎

#### Lemma 2.7.

Consider discretely self-similar data as in Definition 2.1. Then, the following holds:

- 1. The quantity $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r$ is discretely self-similar on $C_{0}^{-}$ :

$$ \Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(u,0)=\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(e^{-\Delta}u,0). $$

(2.16)

- 2. The transverse derivative $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)$ at the bifurcation sphere $p$ is determined by the data on $C_{0}^{-}$ and satisfies

$$ \Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)=\frac{1}{4-4e^{-\Delta(1+\kappa)}}\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}e^{-F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}. $$

(2.17)

- 3. The transverse derivative $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(u,0)$ along $C_{0}^{-}$ is determined by the data on $C_{0}^{-}$ and given as

$$ \Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(u,0)=\frac{e^{F(u)}}{-u}\cdot\bigg(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)-\frac{1}{4}\int_{-1}^{u}e^{-F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}\bigg). $$

(2.18)

- 4. For $0<\kappa\ll 1$ sufficiently small, we have the bounds $\displaystyle\sup_{u\in[-1,0)}\big|4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r-1\big|\lesssim\kappa,\quad\sup_{u\in[-1,0)}|\mu|\lesssim\kappa.$ (2.19)

#### Proof.

The constraint (2.16) follows from

$$ \mu=\frac{2m}{r}=1+4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}r=1-4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r $$

on $C_{0}^{-}$ and the imposed discrete self-similarity condition (2.7) for $\mu$ .

We now use (1.7), (2.15) and $\partial_{u}r=-1$ to compute

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r) \displaystyle=\partial_{u}\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r+\Omega^{-2}\left(\frac{-\Omega^{2}}{4r}-\frac{\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}r}{r}\right) \displaystyle=\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r\left(\partial_{u}\log\Omega^{-2}-\frac{\partial_{u}r}{r}\right)-\frac{1}{4r} \displaystyle=\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r\left(-u(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2}-\frac{1}{u}\right)+\frac{1}{4u}. $$

Using the definition of $F$ we rewrite the above as

$$ \partial_{u}\left(e^{-F(u)+\int_{-1}^{u}\frac{1}{u^{\prime}}du^{\prime}}\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r\right)=\frac{1}{4u}e^{-F(u)+\int_{-1}^{u}\frac{1}{u^{\prime}}du^{\prime}}=-\frac{1}{4}e^{-F(u)}. $$

We integrate from $u=-1$ to $u$ to obtain

$$ (-u)e^{-F(u)}\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(u)-\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)=\int_{-1}^{u}-\frac{1}{4}e^{-F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}. $$

Solving for $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r$ yields (2.18). In order to obtain the formula for $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)$ we use the periodicity of $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r$ and obtain from (2.22) that $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)$ has to satisfy

$$ \Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)(e^{\Delta(-\kappa-1)}-1)=\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}-\frac{1}{4}e^{-F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}. $$

Solving for $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)$ gives (2.17).

To prove the bounds in (2.19), we first observe the bounds

$$ \sup_{u\in[-1,-e^{-\Delta}]}|F|\lesssim\kappa,\quad\sup_{u\in[-1,-e^{-\Delta}]}|e^{-F}-1|\lesssim\kappa,\quad\text{ and }\quad|e^{-\Delta\kappa}-1|\lesssim\kappa. $$

Thus, using (2.17) we obtain

$$ \left|4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)-1\right|=\left|\frac{1}{1-e^{-\Delta-\Delta\kappa}}\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}e^{F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}-1\right|\lesssim\left|\frac{1}{1-e^{-\Delta}}\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}du^{\prime}-1\right|+\kappa=\kappa. $$

Using the above estimates, (2.18) and (2.16) we obtain that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{u\in[-1,0)}|4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(u,0)-1| \displaystyle=\sup_{u\in[-1,-e^{-\Delta}]}|4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(u,0)-1| \displaystyle=\sup_{u\in[-1,-e^{-\Delta}]}\frac{e^{F(u)}}{-u}\left|4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)-\int_{-1}^{u}e^{-F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}+ue^{-F(u)}\right|\lesssim\kappa. $$

The bound on $\mu$ follows from the above and (2.20) which concludes the proof. ∎

Analogously to the rigidity for $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)$ from Lemma 2.7 will now show that the discrete self-similarity for $\frac{\partial_{v}(r\phi)}{\partial_{v}r}$ along $C_{0}^{-}$ constrains $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi$ at the bifurcation sphere $p$ .

#### Lemma 2.8.

Consider discretely self-similar data as in Definition 2.1. Then, the following holds:

- 1. The quantity $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)$ is discretely self-similar on $C_{0}^{-}$

$$ \Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(u,0)=\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(e^{-\Delta}u,0). $$

(2.24)

- 2. The transverse derivative $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)$ at the bifurcation sphere $p$ is determined by the data on $C_{0}^{-}$ and satisfies

$$ \Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)=-\frac{e^{\kappa\Delta}}{1-e^{\kappa\Delta}}\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}\frac{e^{-F(u^{\prime})}}{-4u^{\prime}}\mu(u^{\prime})\phi(u^{\prime})du^{\prime}. $$

(2.25)

- 3. The transverse derivative $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(u,0)$ along $C_{0}^{-}$ is determined by the data on $C_{0}^{-}$ and given as

$$ \Omega^{-2}(u,0)\partial_{v}(r\phi)(u,0)=e^{F(u)}\left(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)-\int_{-1}^{u}\frac{e^{-F(u^{\prime})}}{-4u^{\prime}}\mu(u^{\prime})\phi(u^{\prime})du^{\prime}\right). $$

(2.26)

- 4. For $0<\kappa\ll 1$ sufficiently small, we have the bound

$$ \big|\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)\big|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}. $$

(2.27)

#### Proof.

The first statement (2.24) is a direct consequence of (2.8) and (2.16).

We now write (1.7) as

$$ \partial_{u}\partial_{v}(r\phi)=-\frac{m\Omega^{2}}{2r^{2}}\phi $$

which, after integration and multiplication by $\Omega^{-2}$ , gives

$$ \Omega^{-2}(u,0)\partial_{v}(r\phi)(u,0)=\Omega^{-2}(u,0)\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)-\Omega^{-2}(u,0)\int_{-1}^{u}\frac{\Omega^{2}(u^{\prime},0)}{-4u}\mu\phi du^{\prime}. $$

Evaluating the above at $u=-e^{-\Delta}$ and using (2.24) gives

$$ \Omega^{-2}(p)\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)=\frac{\Omega^{-2}(-e^{-\Delta},0)}{\Omega^{-2}(p)}\Omega^{-2}(p)\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)-\Omega^{-2}(-e^{-\Delta},0)\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}\frac{\Omega^{2}(u^{\prime},0)}{-4u^{\prime}}\mu\phi du^{\prime}. $$

Solving for $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)$ and using (2.13) yields (2.25). Similarly, we obtain

$$ \Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(u,0)=e^{F(u)}\left(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)-\int_{-1}^{u}\frac{e^{-F(u^{\prime})}}{-4u^{\prime}}\mu\phi du^{\prime}\right). $$

To prove (2.27) we first note that

$$ |\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)|\lesssim\frac{1}{\kappa\Delta}\sup_{u\in[-1,-e^{-\Delta}]}|\mu\phi|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}, $$

where we used (2.6) and (2.19). Using the periodicity of $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(u,0)$ and the bounds on $\phi$ and $\mu$ as we did to control $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)$ , we obtain (2.27) which concludes the proof. ∎

#### Remark 2.9.

In Definition 2.1 we require the first transverse derivative of the geometry and scalar field to be discretely self-similar. Analogously, one can define discretely self-similar profiles of higher order $n\geq 1$ . This would impose $n-1$ additional constraints on the higher-order transverse derivatives of the scalar field $\partial_{v}^{i}\phi|_{p}$ and on the radius $\partial_{v}^{i}r|_{p}$ for $i\leq n$ , analogously to Lemma 2.7 and Lemma 2.8.

#### 2.3.2 Estimates along the outgoing cone

We note that along the outgoing cone, we have that

$$ \Omega^{2}(-1,v)=\frac{1}{1-\kappa} $$

which is a consequence of (2.2) and the gauge condition (2.1). The self-similarity imposed on the scalar field means that

$$ \partial_{v}\phi(p)=\frac{-e^{\kappa\Delta}}{(1-\kappa)(1-e^{\kappa\Delta})}\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}\frac{e^{-F(u^{\prime})}}{-4u^{\prime}}\mu(u^{\prime})\phi(u^{\prime})du^{\prime} $$

where we recall that $\phi(p)=0$ .

#### Remark 2.10.

Our arguments also apply if we only require the regularity for $\phi$ to be $C^{1,\gamma}_{v}\big([0,\infty)\big),$ where $\gamma=2\kappa/(1-\kappa).$ We notice that this is the same regularity exponent as in [RS23]. However, while in the examples of [Chr94] and [RS23] restricting the regularity of the spacetime was essential in the construction of the exterior solution, in our case we can already achieve this for a smooth scalar field.

The above choices determine $r$ on $C_{0}^{+}$ by the Raychaudhuri equation (1.9) and the constraints at $p$ :

$$ \begin{cases}\partial_{v}^{2}r=-r(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}\\
r(p)=1,\ \partial_{v}r(p)=\frac{1}{(1-\kappa)(4-4e^{-\Delta(1+\kappa)})}\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}e^{-F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}.\end{cases} $$

We have completed the setup for the characteristic initial data on $C_{0}^{+}.$ Next, we prove estimates on $C_{0}^{+}$ for all the relevant quantities that will be of use later in the proof.

#### Lemma 2.11.

Consider discretely self-similar data as in Definition 2.1. Then, for $0<\kappa\ll 1$ sufficiently small, we have

$$ \bigg|r(-1,v)-1-\partial_{v}r(p)v\bigg|\lesssim\kappa v $$

and

$$ \bigg|\partial_{v}r(-1,v)-\partial_{v}r(p)\bigg|\lesssim\kappa. $$

#### Proof.

We denote $v_{*}=\sup\big\{v\colon\partial_{v}r>0\text{ on }[0,v]\big\},$ and we prove that $v_{*}=\infty.$ Since $\partial_{v}^{2}r(-1,v)<0,$ we have the bound $0\leq\partial_{v}r(-1,v)\leq\partial_{v}r(p)\leq 2$ on $[0,v_{*}),$ which implies that $1\leq r(-1,v)\leq 1+2v$ . From (1.9) get the bound on $[0,v_{*})$ :

$$ \big|\partial_{v}^{2}r(-1,v)\big|\lesssim\kappa\frac{1+2v}{(1+v)^{4}}. $$

We integrate this bound from 0 to obtain that (2.34) holds for all $v\in[0,v_{*}).$ Taking $\kappa$ sufficiently small, we obtain that $v_{*}=\infty$ as desired. Finally, we use (2.34) and the fundamental theorem of calculus to get (2.33). ∎

Next, we prove the following estimate for $\partial_{u}r$ :

#### Lemma 2.12.

Consider discretely self-similar data as in Definition 2.1. Then, for $0<\kappa\ll 1$ sufficiently small, we have

$$ \big|\partial_{u}r(-1,v)+1\big|\lesssim\kappa\frac{v}{v+1} $$

#### Proof.

We rewrite (1.6) as

$$ \partial_{v}\partial_{u}r^{2}=-\frac{1}{2}\Omega^{2} $$

and integrating along on $\{u=-1\}$ gives

$$ r\partial_{u}r+1=-\frac{v}{4(1-\kappa)}, $$

where we have also used the gauge condition (2.32). We can rewrite this equation on $\{u=-1\}$ as

$$ r(\partial_{u}r+1)=r-1-\frac{v}{4(1-\kappa)}=\bigg(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)-\frac{1}{4}\bigg)\frac{v}{1-\kappa}+O(\kappa v)=O(\kappa v), $$

where we also used (2.19) and (2.33). We then divide by $r$ which concludes the proof. ∎

The bounds that we proved so far on the initial data imply the smallness of the Hawking mass:

#### Lemma 2.13.

Consider discretely self-similar data as in Definition 2.1. Then,

$$ m(-1,v)\lesssim\kappa $$

for all $v\in[0,\infty).$

#### Proof.

From $m=\frac{1}{2}\mu r$ and the bound (2.19) we directly obtain $m(p)\lesssim\kappa$ . Plugging the bounds that we proved above for the initial data, we obtain that

$$ 0\leq\partial_{v}m\lesssim\frac{\kappa}{(1+v)^{2}} $$

which shows Lemma 2.13 upon integration. ∎

We also prove the following estimate for $\partial_{u}\phi:$

#### Lemma 2.14.

Consider discretely self-similar data as in Definition 2.1. Then, for $0<\kappa\ll 1$ sufficiently small and for $v\in[0,\infty)$ , we have that

$$ \big|\partial_{u}\phi(-1,v)-\partial_{u}\phi(p)\big|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}\frac{v}{v+1}. $$

#### Proof.

We can rewrite the wave equation (1.7) as $\partial_{v}(r\partial_{u}\phi)=-\partial_{v}\phi\partial_{u}r.$ Thus, on $u=-1$ we have:

$$ r\partial_{u}\phi(-1,v)-r\partial_{u}\phi(p)=O\bigg(\sqrt{\kappa}\frac{v}{v+1}\bigg). $$

We can rewrite this as

$$ r(-1,v)\cdot\big(\partial_{u}\phi(-1,v)-\partial_{u}\phi(p)\big)=-\big(r(-1,v)-1\big)\cdot\partial_{u}\phi(p)+O\big(\sqrt{\kappa}v\big)=O\big(\sqrt{\kappa}v\big), $$

where we also used (2.6) and (2.33). ∎

### 2.4 Proof of Proposition 2.4

#### Proof of Proposition 2.4.

Let $\Delta>0$ and $\kappa>0$ be arbitrary. For the seed data along $C_{0}^{-}$ we make the ansatz $\phi=\sqrt{\kappa}\alpha\psi$ for a fixed $\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(-1,e^{-\Delta}),\psi\not\equiv 0$ which we continue self-similarly according to (2.3). This ensures (2.6). By modulating $\alpha$ as a function of $\Delta$ and $\psi$ , we can verify (2.5) by the intermediate value theorem. Thus there exists a constant $C_{data}>0$ only depending on $\Delta$ (and the fixed profile $\psi$ ) satisfying (2.6).

In order to ensure that $\mu$ is self-similar, it suffices to show that $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r$ is self-similar. We specify $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r$ at $p$ according to (2.17). Indeed, using (2.11), we compute

$$ \displaystyle\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r \displaystyle(e^{-\Delta}u,0)=\frac{e^{F(u)}}{-u}e^{\Delta+\kappa\Delta}\left(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)-\frac{1}{4}\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}e^{-F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}-\frac{1}{4}\int_{-e^{-\Delta}}^{e^{-\Delta}u}e^{-F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{e^{F(u)}}{-u}e^{\Delta+\kappa\Delta}\left(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)+\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(p)(e^{\Delta(-\kappa-1)}-1)-\frac{e^{-(1+\kappa)\Delta}}{4}\int_{-1}^{u}e^{-F(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}\right) \displaystyle=\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(u,0) $$

which shows (2.7).

To show (2.8), we specify $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)$ at $p$ according to (2.25). Then, using (2.26) we compute

$$ \displaystyle\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi) \displaystyle(e^{-\Delta}u,0)=e^{F(u)}e^{\kappa\Delta}\left(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)-\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}\frac{e^{-F(u^{\prime})}}{-4u^{\prime}}\mu\phi du^{\prime}-\int_{-e^{-\Delta}}^{e^{-\Delta}u}\frac{e^{-F(u^{\prime})}}{-4u^{\prime}}\mu\phi du^{\prime}\right) \displaystyle=e^{F(u)}e^{\kappa\Delta}\left(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)+\frac{1-e^{\kappa\Delta}}{e^{\kappa\Delta}}\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)-e^{-\kappa\Delta}\int_{-1}^{u}\frac{e^{-F(u^{\prime})}}{-4u^{\prime}}\mu\phi du^{\prime}\right) \displaystyle=\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(u,0) $$

which shows (2.8). Since $|\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}(r\phi)(p)|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}$ , by potentially making $C_{data}$ larger depending only on $\Delta$ and the choice of $\psi$ , we readily find data $\phi=\sqrt{\kappa}\tilde{\psi}$ on $C_{0}^{+}$ satisfying (2.8). The condition (2.9) follows now from (2.8) and the discrete self-similarity of $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r$ shown above. Note that the gauge $\Omega^{2}=\frac{1}{1-\kappa}$ in $C_{0}^{+}$ uniquely determines $r$ on $C_{0}^{+}$ . ∎

## 3 Construction of the exterior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$

In this section we will prove our main result Theorem 1. Throughout Section 3 we fix the parameter $\Delta>0$ . We also introduce an additional parameter

$$ 0<\delta\ll 1 $$

which is small and independent of all other parameters. For instance, setting $\delta=10^{-5}$ would work for our proof. We consider discretely self-similar characteristic data with period $\Delta$ for ( $r,\Omega^{2},\phi$ ) on $C_{0}^{-}\cup_{p}C_{0}^{+}$ as defined in Definition 2.1. According to Proposition 2.4, there exists a $C_{data}(\Delta)>0$ such that for all $\kappa>0$ , and $N\geq 1$ , there exists such nontrivial discretely self-similar characteristic data with period $\Delta$ . For the rest of Section 3 we fix the parameters

$$ \delta,\Delta,C_{data}(\Delta),\text{ and }N $$

and we will use the following convention. For non-negative quantities $A$ and $B$ , we write $A\lesssim B$ (or also $A=O(B)$ ) if there exists a constant $\tilde{C}>0$ only depending on $\delta$ , $\Delta$ , and $C_{data}(\Delta)$ such that $A\leq\tilde{C}B$ . We will also write “for sufficiently small $A>0$ ” if there exists a constant $A_{0}>0$ sufficiently small and only depending on $\delta$ , $\Delta$ , and $C_{data}(\Delta)$ such that $A$ satisfies $0<A\leq A_{0}$ . Similarly, we write “for sufficiently small $A>0$ depending on $B$ ” if there exists a constant $A_{0}>0$ sufficiently small and only depending on $\delta$ , $\Delta$ , $C_{data}(\Delta)$ and $B$ such that $A$ satisfies $0<A\leq A_{0}$ .

#### Hierarchy of scales

In the proofs in Section 3 we will introduce further parameters of different scales. Our hierarchy of scales is

$$ \kappa(\delta,\underline{v},D)\ll\frac{1}{D(\delta,\underline{v})}\ll\underline{v}(\delta)\ll\delta\ll 1, $$

where we suppressed the additional dependence on the parameters $\Delta,C_{data},k$ occurring in (3.2). We will also make use of $\epsilon\doteq 40\delta$ and $\eta\doteq 10\epsilon=400\delta$ .

By standard local existence results (see e.g. [Daf05, Proposition 1.1]), data as in Definition 2.1 give rise to a unique solution

$$ (r,\Omega^{2},\phi)\in C^{N+2}(\mathcal{R}_{0})\times C^{N+1}(\mathcal{R}_{0})\times C^{N+1}(\mathcal{R}_{0}) $$

in the domain

$$ \mathcal{R}_{0}=\big\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[0,v_{*}(u)]\big\} $$

for some function $v_{*}(u)>0$ . A priori, however, we have no control on the size of this domain as $u\rightarrow 0$ .

#### The decomposition of $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ into the regions $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ – $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$

In order to show Theorem 1 we have to show that $(r,\Omega^{2},\phi)$ extends to the whole domain $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ . Of course, the difficulty is to show existence as uniqueness follows readily. To show existence in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ we will split up the region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ into four regions $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ – $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ and treat each region independently, see Fig. 4. This decomposition was first established in [RS23] and also used in [Sin24]. We begin with region $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ .

### 3.1 Region $\mathcal{R}_{I}$

We define

$$ \mathcal{R}_{I}\doteq\bigg\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[0,\underline{v}^{1-\kappa}],\ \frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\leq\underline{v}^{1-\kappa}\bigg\}, $$

which depends on a small parameter $\underline{v}>0$ .

#### Proposition 3.1.

For $\underline{v}>0$ sufficiently small and $\kappa>0$ sufficiently small depending on $\underline{v}$ , the solution $(r,\Omega^{2},\phi)$ of (3.4) exists in region $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ . Moreover, $(r,\Omega^{2},\phi)$ satisfies the estimates (3.10)–(3.14) in region $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ .

We will prove Proposition 3.1 as a consequence of Proposition 3.2 below at the end of Section 3.1.

#### Bootstrap Assumptions

Our proof will be based on a bootstrap argument and we will now formulate the bootstrap assumptions.

We consider the following bootstrap assumptions

#### Proposition 3.2.

#### Lemma 3.3.

$$ \widetilde{\psi}(u,v):=\psi(u,v)-\psi(u,0) $$

We begin by improving assumption (3.9). Notice that we have the equation:

$$ \partial_{u}\partial_{v}\log\frac{1-\kappa}{|u|^{\kappa}}\Omega^{2}=-2\partial_{u}\phi\partial_{v}\phi+\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2r^{2}}+\frac{2\partial_{v}r\partial_{u}r}{r^{2}}=-2\partial_{u}\phi\partial_{v}\phi+\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2r^{2}}\bigg(1+4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r\partial_{u}r\bigg)= $$

$$ \bigg|\partial_{v}\log\frac{1-\kappa}{|u|^{\kappa}}\Omega^{2}\bigg|=O\big(\kappa\cdot|u|^{-1+\kappa}\big) $$

By choosing $\underline{v}$ sufficiently small we improve the constant in (3.9). Thus, we proved (3.14).

We improve assumption (3.6) next. We have by equation (1.9), together with the bootstrap assumptions and the preliminary estimates:

$$ \big|\widetilde{\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r}\big|\leq\int_{0}^{v}r\cdot\Omega^{2}\cdot\big(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi\big)^{2}(u,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}\lesssim\int_{0}^{v}\kappa\cdot|u|^{\kappa-1}dv^{\prime}\lesssim\kappa\cdot\frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}, $$

which improves assumption (3.6) as before. Thus, we proved (3.11).

We improve assumption (3.7). From the wave equation (1.7), the bootstrap assumptions, and the preliminary estimates we have that

$$ \big|\widetilde{r\partial_{u}\phi}\big|(u,v)\leq\int_{0}^{v}\big|\partial_{u}r\big|\cdot\Omega^{2}\cdot\big|\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi\big|dv^{\prime}\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}\cdot\frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}. $$

$$ r(u,v)\cdot\big|\widetilde{\partial_{u}\phi}\big|\leq\big|\widetilde{r\partial_{u}\phi}\big|(u,v)+\big|\widetilde{r}\big|(u,v)\cdot\big|\partial_{u}\phi\big|(u,0)\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}\cdot\frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}, $$

where we used the previous bound for $\widetilde{r\partial_{u}\phi},$ the bound on initial data for $\partial_{u}\phi(u,0)$ , and the preliminary bound for $\widetilde{r}(u,v).$ This improves assumption (3.7) as before, so we obtain (3.12).

We improve assumption (3.8). Note that we can write equation (1.6) as:

$$ \partial_{v}\big(r\cdot\widetilde{\partial_{u}r}\big)=-\frac{\Omega^{2}}{4}+\partial_{v}r=\Omega^{2}\cdot\bigg(\widetilde{\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r}(u,v)+\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r(u,0)-\frac{1}{4}\bigg)=O\big(\kappa\cdot|u|^{\kappa}\big) $$

$$ \widetilde{\partial_{u}r}=O\bigg(\kappa\cdot\frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\bigg) $$

$$ \partial_{u}\big(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi\big)=-\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi\cdot\bigg(\frac{\partial_{u}r}{r}-\partial_{u}\log\Omega^{-2}\bigg)-\frac{1}{r}\partial_{u}\phi\cdot\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r $$

$$ \partial_{u}\left(\widetilde{\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi}\right)+\widetilde{\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi}\cdot\big(\partial_{u}\log r(u,0)-F^{\prime}(u)\big)\\

$$ |\widetilde{\partial_{u}\log\Omega^{-2}}|\lesssim\kappa|u|^{-2+\kappa}v $$

which together with the bootstrap assumptions and the preliminary estimates, gives us

$$ \partial_{u}\left(\widetilde{\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi}\right)+\widetilde{\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi}\cdot\big(\partial_{u}\log r(u,0)-F^{\prime}(u)\big)=O\bigg(\sqrt{\kappa}\cdot|u|^{-2}\frac{v^{\frac{1-\kappa-\delta}{1-\kappa}}}{|u|^{1-\kappa-\delta}}\bigg) $$

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi}|(u,v) \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{e^{F(u)}}{|u|}\cdot|\widetilde{\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi}|(-1,v)+\frac{e^{F(u)}}{|u|}\cdot\int_{-1}^{u}\frac{|u^{\prime}|}{e^{F(u^{\prime})}}\cdot\sqrt{\kappa}\cdot|u^{\prime}|^{-2}\cdot\frac{v^{\frac{1-\kappa-\delta}{1-\kappa}}}{|u^{\prime}|^{1-\kappa-\delta}}du^{\prime} \displaystyle\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}\cdot\frac{v}{|u|^{1+\kappa}}+\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}}{|u|^{1+\kappa}}\cdot\int_{-1}^{u}|u^{\prime}|^{-1+\kappa}\cdot\frac{v^{\frac{1-\kappa-\delta}{1-\kappa}}}{|u^{\prime}|^{1-\kappa-\delta}}du^{\prime} \displaystyle\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}\cdot\frac{v}{|u|^{1+\kappa}}+\sqrt{\kappa}\cdot|u|^{-1}\cdot\frac{v^{\frac{1-\kappa-\delta}{1-\kappa}}}{|u|^{1-\kappa-\delta}} $$

where we used the initial data estimates (2.10) and (2.12). Since $1\leq|u|^{-1}$ and $\underline{v}^{\delta}\ll 1,$ we proved (3.10). This completes the proof of Proposition 3.2. ∎

### 3.2 Region $\mathcal{R}_{II}$

In this section we prove the existence of the solution in region $\mathcal{R}_{II}$ . As explained in the introduction, we consider a new system of double null coordinates $(u,V)$ , with respect to which the solution is close to Minkowski space in standard null coordinates. We define on $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}\setminus\mathcal{R}_{I}$ the new coordinates

$$ V(u,v)=v^{\frac{1}{1-\kappa}},\quad u(u,v)=u, $$

in mild abuse of notation. We remark that the associated transition map is a smooth diffeomorphism on $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}\setminus\mathcal{R}_{I}$ and the metric is given by

$$ g=-\bar{\Omega}^{2}(u,V)dudV+r^{2}d\sigma_{S^{2}}, $$

where the new lapse function $\bar{\Omega}^{2}$ is given as

$$ \bar{\Omega}^{2}(u,V)=(1-\kappa)\cdot V^{-\kappa}\cdot\Omega^{2}(u,v(V)). $$

We define

$$ \mathcal{R}_{II}=\bigg\{(u,V):\ u\in[-1,0),\ V\in[0,\underline{v}^{-1}],\ \underline{v}\leq\frac{V}{|u|}\leq\underline{v}^{-1}\bigg\} $$

and the main result of this section is

#### Proposition 3.4.

#### Proposition 3.5.

#### Lemma 3.6.

The area radius function $r$ satisfies:

$$ r(u,V)=\frac{V}{4}-u+O(|u|\kappa^{1-11\delta}) $$

We improve the bootstrap assumptions, completing the proof of Proposition 3.5. We begin by improving assumption (3.23). We can rewrite the wave equation (1.7) as:

$$ \partial_{u}\bigg(\exp\bigg(D\cdot\frac{V}{u}\bigg)r\partial_{V}\phi\bigg)=-D\cdot\frac{V}{u^{2}}\cdot\exp\bigg(D\cdot\frac{V}{u}\bigg)r\partial_{V}\phi-\exp\bigg(D\cdot\frac{V}{u}\bigg)\partial_{V}r\partial_{u}\phi $$

Next, we improve assumption (3.25). We can rewrite the Raychaudhuri equation (1.9) as:

$$ \partial_{V}\bigg(\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\partial_{V}r-\frac{1}{4}\bigg)=-r\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\big(\partial_{V}\phi\big)^{2} $$

$$ \bigg|\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\partial_{V}r-\frac{1}{4}\bigg|(u,V)\leq\bigg|\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\partial_{V}r-\frac{1}{4}\bigg|(u,-\underline{v}u)+\int_{-\underline{v}u}^{V}r\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\big(\partial_{V}\phi\big)^{2}(u,V^{\prime})dV^{\prime} $$

As a result, we obtain that:

$$ \bigg|\exp\bigg(D\cdot\frac{V}{u}\bigg)\cdot\bigg(\partial_{V}r-\frac{1}{4}\bigg)\bigg|\leq\bigg|\bar{\Omega}^{2}\cdot\exp\bigg(D\cdot\frac{V}{u}\bigg)\cdot\bigg(\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\partial_{V}r-\frac{1}{4}\bigg)\bigg|+\frac{1}{4}\bigg|\exp\bigg(D\cdot\frac{V}{u}\bigg)\cdot\big(\bar{\Omega}^{2}-1\big)\bigg|\leq 2\kappa^{1-10\delta} $$

We point out that since we use the bootstrap assumption (3.27) in the above inequality, the assumption (3.25) must have a lower power of $\kappa$ than (3.27). Also, we remark that a completely analogous proof improves assumption (3.26). Thus, we proved (3.30) and (3.31).

Finally, we improve assumption (3.27). The key point is that we avoid using the estimates (3.25) and (3.26) (which do not have small enough powers of $\kappa$ for our purposes) by using the Hawking mass instead. We use that $\bar{\Omega}^{-2}(-\partial_{u}r)=\frac{1-\mu}{4\partial_{V}r}$ and substitute it in (1.10) to obtain

$$ \partial_{V}m=\big(2\partial_{V}r\big)^{-1}\cdot\bigg(1-\frac{2m}{r}\bigg)\cdot r^{2}(\partial_{V}\phi)^{2}. $$

Using the bootstrap assumptions and the preliminary estimates, we get that $|\partial_{V}m|\leq\kappa^{1-3\delta}.$ Also, by the bounds on the hypersurface $\{V=-\underline{v}u\},$ we have $\frac{m}{r}(u,-\underline{v}u)=O(\kappa).$ Therefore, we have that in region $\mathcal{R}_{II}$ :

$$ \frac{m}{r}\leq\kappa^{1-4\delta} $$

The relation between (3.27) and the Hawking mass follows from the equation

$$ \partial_{u}\partial_{V}\log\bar{\Omega}^{2}=-2\partial_{u}\phi\partial_{V}\phi+\frac{\bar{\Omega}^{2}}{r^{2}}\cdot\frac{m}{r}. $$

Using the bootstrap assumptions and the bound for the Hawking mass, we obtain that:

$$ \big|\partial_{u}\partial_{V}\log\bar{\Omega}^{2}\big|\leq|u|^{-2}\kappa^{1-5\delta} $$

We claim that the analysis in region $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ implies that $\partial_{u}\log\Omega^{2}\big(u,|\underline{v}u|^{1-\kappa}\big)=O(\kappa|u|^{-1}).$ Indeed, we already proved that $\widetilde{\partial_{u}\log\Omega^{2}}=O(\kappa|u|^{-1})$ and $\partial_{u}\log\Omega^{2}(u,0)=O(\kappa|u|^{-1}).$ Moreover, we notice that we also have $\partial_{u}\log\Omega^{2}\big(u,|\underline{v}u|^{1-\kappa}\big)=\partial_{u}\log\bar{\Omega}^{2}(u,-\underline{v}u).$ Thus, we integrate the above in the $V$ direction in order to get:

$$ \big|\partial_{u}\log\bar{\Omega}^{2}\big|\leq V^{-1}\kappa^{1-6\delta}. $$

Finally, we integrate this in the $u$ direction and use the bounds on $\log\bar{\Omega}^{2}$ on the hypersurfaces $\big\{V=-\underline{v}u\big\}$ and $\big\{u=-1,\ V\in[\underline{v},\underline{v}^{-1}]\big\}$ to get:

$$ \big|\log\bar{\Omega}^{2}\big|\leq\kappa^{1-7\delta} $$

This implies that

$$ \big|\bar{\Omega}^{2}-1\big|\cdot\exp\bigg(D\cdot\frac{V}{u}\bigg)\leq\kappa^{1-8\delta} $$

improving assumption (3.27) and proving (3.32). This completes the proof of Proposition 3.5.∎

$$ \partial_{u}\bigg(r\bigg(\partial_{V}r-\frac{1}{4}\bigg)\bigg)=-\frac{\bar{\Omega}^{2}}{4}\cdot\big(\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\partial_{u}r+1\big) $$

We integrate this and use the bootstrap assumptions, the preliminary estimates, and the bounds of the solution on $\{u=-\underline{v}V\}$ in order to get:

$$ r\bigg|\partial_{V}r-\frac{1}{4}\bigg|\leq\frac{1}{2}V\kappa^{1-\epsilon}+O\bigg(\kappa^{1-2\epsilon}\int_{-\underline{v}V}^{u}\bigg|\frac{V}{u^{\prime}}\bigg|^{\frac{p}{2}}du^{\prime}\bigg)\leq\frac{1}{2}V\kappa^{1-\epsilon}+O\big(V\kappa^{1-2\epsilon}\underline{v}^{1-\frac{p}{2}}\big)\leq V\kappa^{1-2\epsilon} $$

We improve the assumption (3.40). We have from the Raychaudhuri equation (1.8):

$$ \big|\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\partial_{u}r+1\big|(u,V)\leq\big|\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\partial_{u}r+1\big|(-\underline{v}V,V)+\int_{-\underline{v}V}^{u}r\bar{\Omega}^{-2}(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2}(u^{\prime},V)du^{\prime} $$

$$ \big|rV^{\kappa}\partial_{V}\phi\big|\leq C\kappa^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\eta}{2}}+|\phi V^{\kappa}\partial_{V}r|+O\bigg(\int_{-1}^{u}\kappa^{1-\epsilon}V^{-2+2\kappa}|u^{\prime}|^{-\frac{p}{2}}du^{\prime}\bigg)\leq\kappa^{\frac{1}{2}-2\eta}. $$

Using equation (3.34) and the previously established bounds, we obtain

$$ \big|\partial_{V}\log V^{\kappa}\bar{\Omega}^{2}\big|=O\bigg(\int_{-1}^{u}\kappa^{1-4\eta}V^{-2+\kappa}|u^{\prime}|^{-p}du^{\prime}\bigg)=O\big(\kappa^{1-4\eta}V^{-2+\kappa}\big). $$

Since we obtain enough decay in $V,$ we integrate this bound and use (3.52) to obtain (3.59). ∎

### 3.5 Proof of Theorem 1

Finally, the estimates that we proved so far allow us to complete the proof of Theorem 1:

#### Proof of Theorem 1.

By construction, the solution satisfies the discrete self-similarity conditions (1.3) on $C_{0}^{-}$ . Our analysis of the solution in regions $\mathcal{R}_{I},\mathcal{R}_{II},\mathcal{R}_{III},$ and $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ proves that the solution exists in the exterior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ . Moreover, the affine length of $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ is given (see [Daf05a]) by

$$ \lim_{v\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-1}^{0}\frac{\Omega^{2}(u,v)}{\Omega^{2}(-1,v)}du=\lim_{V\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-1}^{0}\frac{\bar{\Omega}^{2}(u,V)}{\bar{\Omega}^{2}(-1,V)}du=\lim_{V\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-1}^{0}V^{\kappa}\bar{\Omega}^{2}(u,V)du. $$

We use the bound (3.59) in order to get:

$$ \lim_{V\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-1}^{0}V^{\kappa}\bar{\Omega}^{2}(u,V)du\leq\lim_{V\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-1}^{0}e^{\kappa^{1-5\eta}}|u|^{-p}du\lesssim 1. $$

In conclusion, the spacetime $\big(M,g\big)$ has a future incomplete $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ . ∎
